summary: SQLite WAL checkpointing controls how the write‑ahead log is flushed to the database file. Automatic checkpoints occur after a configurable number of pages, while manual checkpoints can be invoked via PRAGMA or the C API with distinct modes that affect writer blocking and WAL file truncation. Recent bugs around race conditions have been fixed, improving reliability of checkpoint operations.

claims.text: SQLite automatically triggers a checkpoint after 1000 WAL pages (≈4 MiB) have been written, unless overridden by PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint or sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint().

Manual checkpointing is available through the C API sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 and PRAGMA wal_checkpoint, supporting modes PASSIVE (no writer blocking), FULL (blocks writers until checkpoint finishes), RESTART (blocks and resets WAL header), and TRUNCATE (blocks and truncates the WAL file after checkpoint).
Long‑running readers can starve checkpoints, causing WAL file growth; increasing the frequency of automatic checkpoints via PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint mitigates this issue.
The WAL‑Reset race bug, which could silently lose data when a checkpoint raced with a writer, existed through SQLite 3.51.2 and was fixed in SQLite 3.51.3 (released March 2026).

sources.title: Antithesis Blog: Reproducing SQLite WAL Checkpoint Race

open_questions: Will future SQLite releases adjust the default autocommit checkpoint threshold beyond 1000 pages?
